The Air: It's Harder to Breathe in the City

Air quality is an abstract concept that often gets overlooked until it affects our daily lives. It's present everywhere, always, but its impact can only be felt in extreme conditions. The quality of air we breathe is determined by various elements, but the result is the same – we're all connected through this invisible substance.

Remembering the Air

I recall an incident during childhood when I visited my grandmother in the countryside. It was hot, and the roads to her house were made out of gravel and sand. The wind would scatter the particles across the road, raising clouds of dust as we walked. My grandmother's eyes would squint, and she'd cover her mouth in an attempt to minimize exposure. Most kids would be jumping around freely, unaware of the tiny projectiles dancing in the air.

In contrast, breathing in cities feels different for similar reasons. Cars, factories, and construction sites all release toxic chemicals into the atmosphere, but instead of getting a dust-filled haze, there's a thick layer of pollutants that makes the air harder to inhale. Many people can't pinpoint the exact cause of their allergy or asthma, but living in cities might be a more contributing factor than they think.

As technology advances, hang gliding and other adventure sports become increasingly popular. Gravity is still a binding force that restricts our movement in the world but allowing humans to glide freely is an improvement no matter how you look at it.

The skies above metropolises however are subject to smog or heavy pollution depending on the geographical area and other factors. The air's temperature, water vapor content, and acidity level also determine its quality. Deforestation, marsh fires, desertification, agricultural runoff, and release of CO2 contributes significantly.

There's largely been little if any improvement. In general, the disease spread of indoor contagion systems (SARS, Influenza, Tuberculosis) have lasting impacts for patients that survive these crippling breaks.
